Question: The two roots of the equation \[ \begin{aligned} a(b-c)x^2+b(c-a)x\\ {}+c(a-b)&=0 \end{aligned} \] are \(1\) and:
Solution:
Work in the quadratic setting indicated by “the two roots,” so assume \(a(b-c)\ne0\). The roots need not be distinct. Set
\[
p=a(b-c),\qquad q=c(a-b).
\]
The coefficient identity
\[
a(b-c)+b(c-a)+c(a-b)=0
\]
shows that the coefficient of \(x\) is \(-(p+q)\). This lets us group terms to expose the known root \(1\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
p x^2-(p+q)x+q
&=p x(x-1)-q(x-1)\\
&=(x-1)(p x-q).
\end{aligned}
\]
A product is zero when at least one factor is zero. Thus the roots are \(1\) and \(q/p\), with division valid because \(p\ne0\). If \(q=p\), both roots are \(1\); if \(q=0\), the other root is \(0\).

The nonzero-leading-coefficient condition matters. If \(p=0\), the equation becomes \(q(1-x)=0\): it has only the root \(1\) when \(q\ne0\), and every \(x\) satisfies it when \(q=0\). Those are not two-root quadratic cases. In the stated quadratic setting, the other root is therefore
\[
\boxed{\frac{c(a-b)}{a(b-c)}},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
